headline: The PEG Paradox: Why the Semiconductor Sector's Cheapest Names May Also Be Its Most Obvious
lede: A ranking of thirty semiconductor giants by forward PEG ratio — a metric dividing next-year earnings multiples by projected earnings growth — reveals something the headline valuations conceal: several of the sector's most storied names are priced as though their earnings supercycle has already ended.
body:
The table that @bubbleboi circulated arranges thirty semiconductor companies by forward P/E (the price an investor pays today per dollar of next-year earnings) and then divides that multiple by the expected EPS growth rate to produce a forward PEG ratio. A PEG below 1.0 conventionally signals that the market is not fully compensating investors for the growth embedded in consensus estimates — in other words, the stock is cheap relative to what it is expected to earn. By that standard, the top of this list is extraordinary. SK Hynix trades at 4.3 times next-year earnings against 23% expected EPS growth, yielding a PEG of 0.18. Micron, the American memory incumbent, sits at 5.4x on nearly 70% projected EPS growth, producing a PEG of 0.08 — effectively a rounding error. These are not obscure micro-caps; SK Hynix and Micron together represent over $1.2 trillion in combined market capitalisation and form the backbone of the global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supply chain that every AI accelerator depends upon.

The explanation for such depressed multiples is not a mystery; it is a memory cycle scar. DRAM and NAND flash markets are famously cyclical, prone to inventory gluts that crater prices and earnings within a matter of quarters. Investors who lived through the 2022–2023 downturn — when Micron's EPS swung from roughly $8 to deeply negative — apply a structural discount to memory names, treating their earnings as temporarily elevated rather than durably compounding. The irony is that 2026 looks nothing like prior troughs: SK Hynix reported Q1 2026 revenue up 198% year-on-year, HBM capacity is reportedly fully committed through the year, and Morgan Stanley lifted its 2026 and 2027 earnings forecasts for SK Hynix by 56% and 63% respectively. The market's cyclical discount persists even as the cycle itself may be structurally different — one driven by AI infrastructure demand that carries longer lead times and stickier purchase commitments than the consumer electronics cycles of the past.

NVIDIA occupies a fascinating position in the middle of the table. At 17.5x forward earnings on 34.8% projected EPS growth, its PEG of 0.50 places it among the cheapest large-cap technology franchises on the planet — cheaper on this measure than Applied Materials, TSMC, Broadcom, or any of the semiconductor equipment names. The company delivered $216 billion in fiscal-year revenue for FY2026, up 65% year-on-year, and its hyperscaler customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta — have collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capital expenditure for 2026 alone. That NVIDIA's forward multiple has compressed to 17x reflects the market's growing uncertainty about whether current spending levels are sustainable rather than any deterioration in the underlying franchise.

At the other end of the spectrum, ARM Holdings stands in a category of its own: 98.5x next-year earnings against only 21% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 4.67 — the most expensive name on the list by a wide margin, and a figure that GuruFocus placed even higher (above 110x) as of late April 2026. ARM's premium reflects the thesis that it is not merely a chip designer but the inevitable royalty collector of every compute device on earth, from smartphones to AI servers. That thesis may be correct, but at a PEG of 4.67, investors are paying for decades of future royalty streams today. Monolithic Power Systems (PEG 2.95) and Analog Devices (PEG 2.05) sit in similarly stretched territory, their defensive, industrial-facing revenue profiles commanding premium multiples that leave little room for earnings disappointment.

Two names deserve particular scrutiny for structural reasons. Intel's 101% projected EPS growth looks dramatic but is arithmetically trivial to achieve: it is bouncing off a near-zero earnings base following years of execution stumbles and the $7 billion charge associated with its foundry restructuring under successive CEOs. Q1 2026 delivered $13.6 billion in revenue with non-GAAP EPS of $0.29 — a genuine beat against a consensus that had modelled something close to breakeven — and the data-centre division grew 22%, but the 101% growth figure tells an investor almost nothing about whether Intel's normalised earnings power justifies its $500 billion valuation. Marvell presents a mirror image problem: the table shows 0.2% next-year EPS growth against a 42.1x forward multiple, rendering its PEG not-meaningful. Yet Marvell's fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS grew 81% year-on-year, suggesting that the near-zero growth figure reflects a specific transitional period rather than secular stagnation — Marvell's custom silicon and AI networking revenue continues to compound, even if the consensus has yet to catch up.

The broader picture the table draws is one of profound bifurcation. Memory companies trade as though the AI supercycle is a blip; royalty and IP-driven models like ARM trade as though their moat is infinite and already fully monetised. The most interesting opportunities, if the table is taken at face value, sit in the middle: NVIDIA, MediaTek (PEG 0.33), Broadcom (PEG 0.42), AMD (PEG 0.51), and Microchip Technology (PEG 0.49) all combine meaningful scale with forward PEGs well below 1.0, suggesting that the market is either underestimating their earnings durability or overestimating the risks to their growth trajectories. Whether "still so early" describes the AI infrastructure build-out, the market's repricing of that build-out, or simply the memory cycle's second innings is a question the table poses but cannot answer.

concepts.definition: The Price/Earnings-to-Growth ratio using forward (next fiscal year) estimates: forward P/E divided by next-year expected EPS growth rate. A PEG below 1.0 is conventionally considered inexpensive relative to growth; above 1.0 suggests the market is paying a premium for each unit of expected earnings expansion.

The price-to-earnings multiple calculated using next fiscal year's consensus earnings estimate rather than trailing reported earnings. It reflects what investors are willing to pay today for each dollar of expected future profit, and is the standard valuation shorthand for growth-stage technology and semiconductor companies.

A stacked DRAM architecture that delivers far greater data throughput per watt than conventional memory, and is the primary memory type used in AI accelerators like NVIDIA's H100 and B200. SK Hynix and Micron are the leading HBM suppliers, with SK Hynix currently holding the largest share of NVIDIA allocations.

Year-over-year percentage change in earnings per share. In cyclical industries like semiconductors, EPS growth rates can be dramatically distorted by the base period — a company recovering from a loss year can show triple-digit growth even with modest absolute earnings improvement.

fact_check: Intel's 101% projected EPS growth is a base-effect artifact: the company was near breakeven in fiscal 2025 after restructuring charges, so even a modest return to profitability produces a large percentage gain. Q1 2026 EPS came in at $0.29 non-GAAP vs. near-zero consensus, and full-year 2026 estimates range from $0.48–$0.56, making the 101% figure plausible but largely uninformative about normalised earning power. Marvell's 0.2% next-year EPS growth (N.M. PEG) contrasts sharply with its fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS growth of 81% — the flat consensus likely reflects a transitional quarter or fiscal-year boundary effect rather than a business plateau; Marvell's data-centre revenue reached 74% of total sales driven by AI networking ASICs. QUALCOMM's negative EPS growth (-0.3%) reflects the expected partial loss of Apple modem revenue as Apple transitions to in-house chips, partially offset by record automotive revenue ($1.3B in Q2 FY2026, +38% YoY). ARM's forward P/E of 98.5x in this table aligns with third-party estimates ranging from 90x to 121x as of April–May 2026 depending on methodology.
